title: Tutoring & Test Preparation Franchises
one_liner: A mature, low-concentration education-franchise niche is being pulled between post-pandemic learning recovery, renewed selective-college testing requirements, and faster-growing online tutoring substitutes.
overview: The industry consists of franchised tutoring and test-prep centers that provide academic support and exam preparation while excluding online-only tutoring operators. The 2022 IBIS baseline placed revenue at $1.669 billion, profit at $139 million and establishments at 4,250, with 2022 revenue growth of 2.3% and a 2022-2027 forecast CAGR of 2.0%. A 2025 current estimate of about $1.77 billion follows that baseline forecast path, while 2026 demand is shaped by three visible forces: persistent K-12 learning gaps, the digital SAT and renewed test requirements at some selective colleges, and online tutoring growth that is expanding faster than brick-and-mortar franchise centers.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimate: $1.77 billion in US tutoring and test preparation franchise revenue, inferred from the 2022 IBIS baseline of $1.669 billion and the 2022-2027 forecast CAGR of 2.0%.
key_stats.growth: 2025 estimate: about 2.0% annual revenue growth for the franchise-defined industry, aligned with the 2022-2027 IBIS forecast CAGR.
key_stats.profit: 2022 baseline: $139 million profit and an 8.3% profit margin.
key_stats.online_substitute_market: 2024: US online tutoring services revenue was $2.3125 billion; 2025-2030 expected CAGR was 10.1%.
key_stats.sat_participation: 2024: more than 1.97 million students in the high school class of 2024 took the SAT at least once, up from 1.91 million in 2023.
key_stats.learning_gap_indicator: 2024 NAEP results released in 2025 showed 45% of 12th graders below NAEP Basic in math and 32% below NAEP Basic in reading.

baseline_2022.growth: 2022: 2.3% annual revenue growth; 2017-2022 CAGR: 2.1%; 2022-2027 forecast CAGR: 2.0%.
baseline_2022.service_mix: 2022: math tutoring was 42.9% of revenue; reading and writing tutoring was 23.0%; science tutoring was 17.3%; foreign language tutoring was 7.5%.

how_it_makes_money: Franchisees earn revenue from recurring center-based and hybrid tutoring memberships, subject-specific programs, diagnostic assessments, SAT/ACT/AP and admissions-test preparation, summer or STEM camps, school partnerships and add-on college-readiness services. Franchisors earn initial franchise fees, ongoing royalties, curriculum/material fees, technology fees and marketing contributions.
cost_structure: The model is labor-heavy but not capital-intensive. The 2022 baseline showed wages of $618 million, equal to about 37.0% of 2022 revenue, and profit of $139 million, equal to an 8.3% 2022 margin. Major remaining costs include rent for learning centers, royalties and marketing fees, curriculum and testing materials, local advertising, software platforms, insurance, utilities and administrative support. Hybrid delivery can reduce classroom utilization pressure, but high-quality tutors and franchise compliance keep labor and overhead meaningful.
major_players: Kumon North America: 2025 public filing data cited 1,637 US stores; Kumon franchise marketing cited 23,000+ learning centers worldwide.
Mathnasium: 2025 company release cited over 1,200 locations across 12 countries, 51 new franchise agreements in the first half of 2025 and 42 global openings in that period.
Sylvan Learning: 2025 franchise materials cited $795,074 average gross sales and 433 points of presence.
Huntington Learning Center: 2026 franchise site positioned the brand as a nationwide network with a new-center investment range beginning at $177,742.
C2 Education: 2026 website cited 130+ centers across the US and Canada, with in-person, hybrid and online services.
Tutor Doctor: 2026 franchise materials emphasized a home-based tutoring model with 2019 FDD-based US initial investment ranges of $94,295-$138,995 for a local license.
current_dynamics: In 2025-2026, demand is strongest where parents can see measurable skill gaps in math, reading and executive function, especially for elementary and middle-school students. Franchise centers benefit from brand trust, local accountability and structured curriculum, but online platforms are growing faster and often compete on convenience and price. Test prep is no longer a simple decline story: 2020-2024 test-optional policies reduced urgency, but 2025-2027 reinstatements at selective institutions and the 2024 digital SAT transition are reviving demand for targeted prep among college-bound families.
whats_growing: Math remediation, reading intervention, high-dosage tutoring partnerships, hybrid center-plus-online delivery, STEM enrichment, digital SAT prep, AP support, executive-function coaching and franchise concepts that can sell recurring subscriptions instead of one-off homework help.
whats_shrinking: Purely in-person-only tutoring models, generic test-prep packages for broad-access colleges, low-differentiation homework help, centers dependent on one local school catchment, and operators unable to match online scheduling flexibility or demonstrate learning gains.
recent_developments: 2024-03: College Board launched the fully digital SAT in the US, with more than 200,000 weekend test takers and more than 400,000 school-day SAT-suite test takers in the launch week.
2024-09: College Board reported 1.97 million class-of-2024 SAT takers, up from 1.91 million in 2023, while the average total score fell to 1024.
2025-07: Mathnasium reported 51 new franchise agreements in the first half of 2025 and 42 new global center openings.
2025-09: The Nation's Report Card reported 2024 post-pandemic declines, including 45% of 12th graders below NAEP Basic in math.
2026-03: The US Department of Education highlighted a wave of SAT/ACT reinstatements for 2025, 2026 and 2027 admissions cycles at selective universities.
2026-05: Yale announced that first-year and transfer applicants would again be required to submit ACT or SAT scores beginning with the next admissions cycle.
outlook: The 2026-2028 outlook is modestly positive for franchised centers but more competitive than the headline education-recovery story suggests. The 2022 IBIS forecast pointed to 2027 revenue of about $1.8 billion and a 2022-2027 CAGR of 2.0%, which remains a reasonable base case for the franchise-defined market. Upside comes from continuing learning-loss recovery, selective-college test reinstatement, digital SAT prep, and school-funded tutoring contracts. Downside comes from faster-growing online tutoring, tighter household budgets for discretionary services, tutor wage pressure and franchisee saturation in affluent suburban markets.

title: Ultrasonic Cleaning Equipment Manufacturing
one_liner: Niche manufacturers make ultrasonic tanks, generators and automated cleaning systems for healthcare, dental, electronics, aerospace, automotive and precision industrial users.
overview: Operators manufacture equipment that uses high-frequency sound waves, heat and aqueous or solvent-based cleaning media to remove contaminants from medical instruments, dental tools, industrial parts, electronics, jewelry and other hard nonporous items. The 2021 IBIS baseline described a 2020 US manufacturing industry with $390.3 million of revenue, 20 establishments, 18 enterprises, 938 employees, $23.0 million of profit and a 6.0% profit margin, with high-capacity ultrasonic cleaners representing 65.1% of 2020 product revenue, medium-capacity cleaners 26.0% and low-capacity cleaners 8.9%. Current 2025-2026 demand remains tied to healthcare procedure volume, sterile processing, dental offices, semiconductor/electronics manufacturing, aerospace, automotive repair and broader industrial production.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 US ultrasonic cleaning market estimated at $515.1 million; 2025 US manufacturing revenue is estimated near $505 million using the IBIS 2020-2025 recovery path and 2026 market checks.
key_stats.growth: 2025-2032 global ultrasonic cleaning market CAGR estimated at 6.3%; 2025-2035 global ultrasonic cleaning equipment CAGR estimated at 5.8%; 2026 global ultrasonic cleaning equipment market growth estimated at 9.5% from $2.72 billion in 2025 to $2.98 billion in 2026.
key_stats.employment: 2020 IBIS baseline employment was 938 workers; 2025 IBIS forecast employment was 1,069 workers.
key_stats.establishments: 2020 IBIS baseline counted 20 establishments and forecast flat establishment count through 2025.
key_stats.domestic_demand: 2020 IBIS baseline domestic demand was $437 million, with imports equal to 12.6% of domestic demand.
key_stats.macro_drivers: 2024 US national health expenditure grew 7.2% to $5.3 trillion; CMS projected 2025-2034 NHE growth at 5.4% per year; June 2026 US manufacturing output was 1.1% above June 2025 and rose at a 4.7% annual rate in Q2 2026.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 estimated US manufacturing revenue of $432.8 million, derived from the IBIS 2020 revenue of $390.3 million and its 2020-2025 forecast CAGR of 5.3%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 estimated growth of +5.3%, using the IBIS 2020-2025 forecast CAGR because the baseline file does not provide a separate 2022 table.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2020 baseline profit margin was 6.0%; no separate 2022 margin was provided in the baseline file.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2020 baseline product mix: high-capacity ultrasonic cleaners 65.1%, medium-capacity cleaners 26.0%, low-capacity cleaners 8.9%.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue from standard benchtop and console cleaners, high-capacity hospital and laboratory systems, multi-stage wash-rinse-dry systems, custom engineered tanks, generators and transducers, plus aftermarket parts, service, detergents, cleaning chemistries, testing, rentals and refurbished equipment. Larger jobs are sold as capital equipment to hospitals, dental groups, medical device makers, aerospace suppliers, electronics plants and industrial maintenance departments, while smaller units move through distributors and direct online sales.
cost_structure: The largest costs are stainless steel, fabricated metal tanks, transducers, generators, heaters, pumps, controls, sensors, wiring, packaging and purchased components, followed by skilled assembly labor, engineering, compliance testing, warranty service, freight and sales support. The 2020 IBIS baseline reported a 6.0% profit margin and flagged steel as a key input; BLS data showed steel mill products PPI rising through 2026, including 2026 monthly increases from January through June, keeping material costs a margin risk.
current_dynamics: Demand is healthier than the pandemic-era baseline because healthcare spending, sterile-processing backlogs, outpatient procedure volume, electronics manufacturing and precision cleaning requirements have recovered. The market is still fragmented and competitive, with US producers defending custom, regulated and service-intensive applications against imported benchtop and midrange systems. Buyers are prioritizing automation, repeatable cleaning validation, lower solvent use, digital controls, multi-frequency capability, reduced downtime and support for complex/lumened instruments.
whats_growing: High-capacity medical and sterile-processing systems; automated multi-tank wash-rinse-dry lines; electronics and conformal-coating maintenance systems; aerospace, defense and semiconductor precision cleaning; systems with PLCs, touchscreens, programmable cycles, diagnostics, filtration and solvent-saving features; aftermarket service, detergents and validation support.
whats_shrinking: Commodity low-capacity benchtop cleaners made in the US; manual and single-function cleaning systems without data capture or automation; price-sensitive dental, jewelry and consumer units exposed to imports; margin contribution from standard stainless equipment when steel and electronics components rise faster than pricing.
recent_developments: 2025-02: Nordson Electronics Solutions introduced the ASYMTEK Select Coat SL-1040 Ultrasonic Cleaning Station for conformal-coating nozzle and needle maintenance.
2025-03: Transparency Market Research estimated the global ultrasonic cleaning equipment market at $2.1 billion in 2024 and projected a 5.8% CAGR for 2025-2035.
2026-01: ResearchAndMarkets/The Business Research Company reported the global ultrasonic cleaning equipment market growing from $2.72 billion in 2025 to $2.98 billion in 2026.
2026-05: MarketGlass estimated the US ultrasonic cleaning market at $515.1 million in 2025 and the global market at $1.8 billion in 2025.
2026-07: The Federal Reserve reported June 2026 US manufacturing output 1.1% above June 2025 and Q2 2026 manufacturing output up at a 4.7% annual rate.
outlook: The industry should grow modestly through 2026 as medical, dental, electronics, aerospace and industrial buyers keep upgrading cleaning capacity and automation, but revenue will remain volatile because purchases are capital-equipment decisions. A reasonable 2026 view is low- to mid-single-digit US revenue growth, with upside from hospital sterile-processing investment, semiconductor/electronics cleaning and defense/aerospace demand, and downside from import competition, delayed capital budgets, tariffs, steel inflation and weaker consumer-facing applications.
themes: Precision cleaning for electronics and aerospace
one_sentence: The US ultrasonic cleaning equipment manufacturing industry is a small, mature, import-exposed manufacturing niche whose growth is being supported by 2025-2026 healthcare spending, sterile-processing demand, electronics production and industrial automation, while steel and component costs pressure margins.

title: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) Manufacturing
one_liner: U.S. UAV manufacturers are moving from niche defense programs toward larger-scale autonomous, attritable, and NDAA-compliant drone production.
overview: U.S. UAV manufacturing remains defense-led, but the demand mix is broadening. The 2021 baseline described an industry recovering from procurement volatility after revenue fell to $3.3 billion in 2021, with growth expected as MQ-4C Triton, MQ-25 Stingray, civil UAV demand, and looser FAA rules supported a rebound. Current 2025-2026 data show stronger structural tailwinds: the FY2026 defense budget request called out $13.4 billion for autonomy and autonomous systems, including $9.4 billion for unmanned and remotely operated aerial vehicles, while the FAA's 2025 BVLOS proposal would reduce the need for individual waivers and expand commercial use cases. At the same time, federal procurement restrictions on covered foreign drones and Blue UAS vetting are pushing government buyers toward domestic or allied supply chains.

key_stats.market_size: 2026 U.S. UAV manufacturing revenue: $4.6 billion baseline forecast; 2026 broader U.S. drone market: $33.4 billion; 2025 narrower U.S. UAV market: $10.754 billion
key_stats.growth: 2021-2026 UAV manufacturing CAGR: 7.1% baseline forecast; 2025-2030 U.S. UAV market CAGR: 8.0%; 2026-2033 U.S. drone market CAGR: 8.3%
key_stats.defense_budget: FY2026 autonomy and autonomous systems request: $13.4 billion, including $9.4 billion for unmanned and remotely operated aerial vehicles and $3.1 billion for counter-UAS
key_stats.commercial_base: 2025 U.S. drone market hardware share: over 60%; 2025 battery-powered drone revenue share: over 52%

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 UAV manufacturing revenue: about $3.5 billion implied from the 2021 baseline revenue of $3.264 billion and 2021-2026 forecast CAGR of 7.1%
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 implied growth: about 7.1% under the baseline 2021-2026 forecast
baseline_2022.context: The baseline report expected revenue to rise from $3.264 billion in 2021 to $4.6 billion in 2026 as defense procurement recovered and civil UAV adoption expanded.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue from airframes, propulsion, avionics, sensors and payload integration, ground-control systems, autonomy software embedded in aircraft, defense R&D contracts, production contracts, spares, sustainment, training, and specialized commercial systems for inspection, mapping, public safety, agriculture, and delivery. Baseline revenue by system component was 46.0% aircraft, 38.0% payloads, and 16.0% ground-control equipment; baseline product mix was 40.7% tactical and low-altitude UAVs, 24.2% civil UAVs, 18.5% MALE UAVs, and 16.6% HALE UAVs.
cost_structure: Costs are weighted toward specialized labor, electronics, propulsion, composite structures, batteries, sensors, testing, compliance, and program management. Baseline 2021 wages were $798 million, equal to about 24.4% of $3.264 billion revenue; 2021 profit was $333 million, or 10.2% of revenue. The baseline forecast 2026 profit margin was 13.8%, but 2025-2026 domestic-content rules, electronics sourcing, secure communications, and production scaling increase working-capital and supplier-qualification costs.
current_dynamics: Demand is being pulled in two directions. Large defense programs still matter, including HALE/MALE platforms, carrier-based UAVs, loyal-wingman aircraft, and ISR systems, but the fastest procurement energy is shifting toward smaller, cheaper, attritable drones, loitering munitions, counter-UAS, autonomy software, and secure domestic supply chains. Civil and public-sector demand is improving as FAA policy moves toward normalized BVLOS operations, drone-in-a-box deployments, inspection, emergency response, and delivery. Competition remains intense because Chinese and other foreign manufacturers dominate low-cost commercial hardware, while U.S. firms compete most strongly in secure, defense-grade, enterprise, and autonomy-heavy platforms.
whats_growing: 2025-2026 growth is strongest in autonomous and semi-autonomous defense aircraft, loitering munitions, counter-UAS, Blue UAS-cleared small drones, public-safety drone-as-first-responder systems, utility and energy inspection, BVLOS-ready platforms, secure communications, domestic batteries and electronics, and software-defined mission systems. The broader U.S. drone market was estimated at $29.326 billion in 2025 and $33.401 billion in 2026, with hardware still the largest 2025 component and services expected to grow faster through 2033.
whats_shrinking: Federal and federally funded demand for covered foreign drones is shrinking after the American Security Drone Act procurement restrictions took effect for delivery, operation, and federal funds in 2025. Legacy procurement of some older platforms is also under pressure: the FY2026 defense budget discussion referenced divesting Gray Eagle UAVs while shifting resources to loitering munitions, launched effects, autonomy, and counter-UAS. Consumer-style commodity drones remain a weak segment for U.S. manufacturers because imports continue to compete aggressively on price.
recent_developments: 2025-05-05: DIU, NORTHCOM, and the Joint Counter-small UAS Office opened a Replicator 2 solicitation for scalable low-collateral counter-UAS defeat capabilities.
2025-08-06: FAA proposed a BVLOS rule intended to normalize beyond-visual-line-of-sight drone operations and expand commercial use cases.
2025-11: CSET reported that most U.S. drone companies focus on small UAVs while only a handful develop larger complex military systems.
2026-03-13: FAR clause 52.240-1 became effective, restricting federal procurement, operation, and funding of UAS from American Security Drone Act-covered foreign entities.
2026-04-24: Skydio announced a $3.5 billion five-year U.S. manufacturing and supply-chain expansion plan, including more than 2,000 Skydio jobs and over $1 billion for domestic suppliers.
2026-06-26: The FY2026 defense budget request included $13.4 billion for autonomy and autonomous systems, including $9.4 billion for unmanned and remotely operated aerial vehicles.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is positive but uneven. Defense demand should remain the anchor as the Pentagon funds autonomy, counter-UAS, collaborative combat aircraft, loitering munitions, and rapid production pathways. Civil growth depends on the timing and final shape of BVLOS rules, Remote ID enforcement, aircraft certification requirements, and local acceptance of drones over people and infrastructure. The biggest upside is a domestic production ramp supported by federal procurement rules and allied demand; the biggest constraint is whether U.S. suppliers can scale batteries, sensors, chips, radios, motors, and airframes at costs close enough to foreign alternatives.

title: Urban Planning Software
one_liner: Urban planning software sells GIS, 3D modeling, analytics, digital-twin and permitting tools to governments, planners, developers and infrastructure teams.
overview: Urban planning software includes GIS, land-use modeling, zoning and scenario analysis, transportation planning, site-feasibility tools, 3D city modeling, BIM-adjacent civil design software, digital twins and permitting workflow platforms. Demand comes primarily from local and state governments, metropolitan planning organizations, civil engineers, architecture and engineering firms, real estate developers, utilities and transportation agencies. The industry remains concentrated around large infrastructure software ecosystems, especially Esri, Autodesk and Bentley, while niche vendors compete with specialized climate-risk, mobility, zoning, parcel and community-engagement tools. The 2025-2026 market is being pulled in two directions: infrastructure and software digitization support demand, but high interest rates, softer construction spending and constrained municipal budgets slow new seat expansion.

key_stats.market_size: 2026: about $3.3 billion in US industry revenue, estimated from the 2022 IBISWorld baseline and its 2022-2027 forecast path.
key_stats.growth: 2026: about 2.3% estimated annual revenue growth; 2022-2027 baseline forecast CAGR was 2.4%.
key_stats.construction_indicator: June 2026: US construction spending was $2.1665 trillion SAAR, down 3.2% from June 2025; private nonresidential construction was $745.3 billion SAAR and public construction was $544.1 billion SAAR.
key_stats.software_investment_indicator: 2025: US private fixed investment in software was $754.773 billion, up from $692.996 billion in 2024.
key_stats.planner_workforce_indicator: 2024: urban and regional planners held about 44,700 US jobs; BLS projected 3% employment growth for 2024-2034.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2022: 23.8% EBIT margin in the IBISWorld baseline, with margin pressure from open-source GIS and internal enterprise tools.

baseline_2022.profit: 2022: $713 million profit, equal to a 23.8% margin.
baseline_2022.forecast: 2027: $3.4 billion revenue forecast in the baseline, implying a 2.4% CAGR from 2022.

how_it_makes_money: Companies make money through SaaS subscriptions, enterprise GIS licenses, named-user seats, cloud credits, CAD/BIM and civil-design bundles, digital-twin modules, implementation services, training, maintenance, support, data integrations and consulting. Large vendors increasingly bundle planning tools into broader professional user tiers or infrastructure suites, while smaller vendors sell project-based analytics, parcel datasets, scenario modeling, public-engagement modules and agency workflow automation.
cost_structure: The largest costs are software engineering, cloud hosting, geospatial data acquisition, product R&D, cybersecurity, sales and customer success, implementation specialists, documentation, support, channel commissions and corporate overhead. Profitability is helped by recurring subscriptions and high gross margins, but pressured by public-sector procurement cycles, data licensing, cloud compute for 3D/digital-twin workloads, AI features, interoperability requirements and competition from open-source GIS.
major_players: CityFormLab/MIT Urban Network Analysis and other open-source GIS ecosystems
current_dynamics: Federal infrastructure programs, smart-mobility grants, digital permitting initiatives and resilience planning keep the software category relevant in 2025-2026. However, June 2026 construction spending was below June 2025, so vendors are relying more on multi-year government programs, utility/transportation asset planning, climate adaptation and workflow modernization than on broad real estate development growth. Procurement is shifting toward integrated cloud platforms: Esri folded ArcGIS Urban into higher-tier Professional Plus licensing in 2025, Autodesk reported FY2026 AECO revenue growth, and Bentley reported 2025 recurring revenue expansion. Open-source GIS, in-house engineering tools and budget limits remain the main price checks.
whats_growing: Cloud GIS, digital twins, 3D city models, infrastructure lifecycle platforms, AI-assisted permitting review, parcel and zoning analytics, climate-risk and flood-planning modules, transit and curb-management tools, public-engagement dashboards, and integrated planning-design-construction data environments are growing. Demand is strongest where agencies need to coordinate infrastructure funding, housing supply, resilience, transportation safety and environmental review across fragmented datasets.
whats_shrinking: Standalone perpetual licenses, isolated desktop-only planning tools, custom one-off municipal systems, manual permitting workflows, static map production, low-value map viewers and tools that cannot interoperate with GIS, BIM, CAD, asset management or open data standards are shrinking. Demand tied to discretionary real estate development is weaker where financing costs and construction pullbacks delay projects.
recent_developments: 2026-08-03: Census reported June 2026 construction spending of $2.1665 trillion SAAR, down 3.2% from June 2025.
2026-08-06: USDOT updated SMART Grants, noting no new funding notices after 2026 appropriations reallocated $204.912 million of unobligated balances while existing awards continue.
2026-07-30: BEA reported private intellectual-property investment growth of 8.8% in Q2 2026 after 13.8% in Q1 2026.
2026-03-03: Autodesk filed FY2026 results showing $7.206 billion total revenue and $3.583 billion AECO revenue, up 22%.
2026-02-26: Bentley reported 2025 ARR of $1.462 billion and Q4 2025 subscription revenue growth of 13.0%.
2025-03-25: Esri announced ArcGIS Urban would be included with ArcGIS Professional Plus from the June 2025 ArcGIS Online update rather than sold as a separate add-on.
outlook: The industry should keep growing through 2027, but at a steadier pace than the pre-2022 adoption surge. A reasonable 2026-2027 outlook is low-single-digit annual US revenue growth, with stronger upside in public infrastructure, transportation safety, utility resilience, digital permitting and climate adaptation, offset by softer private construction and tighter municipal procurement. Vendors with interoperable GIS, CAD/BIM, permitting, asset-management and digital-twin workflows should gain share; narrow point solutions will need strong datasets, clear procurement ROI or integration partnerships.
one_sentence: The US urban planning software industry is a small but strategic planning-tech market supported by public infrastructure programs, resilient software investment and the shift from standalone GIS/CAD tools toward cloud platforms, subscriptions and digital twins.

title: Urethane Foam Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A mature plastics niche supplying foam for furniture, bedding, insulation, autos, packaging and specialty industrial uses.
overview: The industry manufactures flexible, semi-rigid and rigid polyurethane foam products, excluding polystyrene, for cushioning, mattresses, carpet underlay, packaging, building insulation, auto seating, interior trim, filtration, medical and industrial components. Baseline IBISWorld data described a low-import, mature US market with 2021 revenue of $11.774 billion and a 2021-2026 projected CAGR of 1.39%, reaching about $12.6 billion in 2026 in 2021 dollars. Current public market data points to a broader US polyurethane foam market of $12.8 billion in 2025, with a 2026-2034 forecast CAGR of 5.15%, reflecting stronger insulation, packaging, sustainability and lightweighting demand than the older baseline assumed.

key_stats.forecast_market_size: 2034 US polyurethane foam market forecast: $20.0 billion
key_stats.construction_driver: May 2026 US construction spending SAAR: about $2.207 trillion
key_stats.auto_driver: 2025 US franchised light-vehicle dealers sold 16.2 million light-duty vehicles
key_stats.furniture_driver: 2025 US furniture and related product manufacturing sectoral output: $75.339 billion, down from $85.222 billion in 2022
key_stats.input_cost_indicator: June 2026 plastics material and resin manufacturing PPI: 368.751, up from 308.307 in February 2026

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 estimated industry revenue: about $11.94 billion, calculated from the 2021 IBISWorld revenue of $11.774 billion using the 2021-2026 projected CAGR of 1.39%
baseline_2022.context: The 2022 baseline sits just after the 2021 COVID rebound and before the 2023-2025 weakness in domestic furniture manufacturing output.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell foam buns, rolls, molded parts, spray foam systems, laminated boardstock, fabricated cushions, bedding components, packaging inserts and engineered foam assemblies to furniture, mattress, construction, automotive, healthcare, packaging and industrial buyers. Revenue is earned through volume contracts, custom formulation work, fabrication, conversion services, private-label programs and specialty performance grades such as breathable, low-emission, antimicrobial, fire-retardant, recycled-content or higher-resilience foams.

cost_structure.materials: Largest cost category in 2021; polyols, isocyanates, surfactants, additives, flame retardants and blowing agents are tied to petrochemical and resin markets.
cost_structure.labor: 2021 IBISWorld wages: $1.582 billion across 32,198 workers; labor is meaningful because many producers cut, laminate, mold and fabricate foam to customer specifications.
cost_structure.energy_and_utilities: Foam pouring, curing, cutting, ventilation, compression and chemical handling require steady power, heat management and environmental controls.
cost_structure.freight_and_logistics: Bulky, low-density products raise shipping cost sensitivity, favoring regional production footprints near bedding, furniture, auto and construction customers.
cost_structure.compliance_and_r_and_d: 2025 HFC restrictions, VOC concerns, flammability standards and buyer sustainability requirements increase spending on reformulation, testing, documentation and plant controls.
cost_structure.profit: 2021 IBISWorld profit margin: 5.90%; 2026 margins are pressured where resin, MDI and TDI costs move faster than contract pass-throughs.

current_dynamics: In 2025-2026, demand is split by end market. Construction and energy-efficiency retrofits support rigid and spray foam insulation, while 2025 light-vehicle sales of 16.2 million units support molded seating, headliners and acoustic applications. Furniture is the soft spot: BLS/FRED sectoral output for furniture and related product manufacturing fell to $75.339 billion in 2025 from $85.222 billion in 2022. Input costs have become a bigger issue again, with the plastics material and resin manufacturing PPI reaching 368.751 in June 2026 after 308.307 in February 2026. Regulation is also changing formulations: EPA rules beginning January 1, 2025 cap many polyurethane foam blowing-agent uses at a GWP of 150 for manufacture and import.
whats_growing: Rigid and spray foam insulation, low-GWP and low-emission formulations, recycled or bio-based polyol content, specialty packaging, healthcare foams, automotive acoustic and lightweighting applications, and premium bedding foams with breathability or pressure-relief claims.
whats_shrinking: Commodity flexible foam tied to weak US furniture output, low-differentiation slabstock, products dependent on restricted high-GWP blowing agents, and producers unable to pass through 2026 resin and isocyanate cost volatility.
recent_developments: 2025: IMARC estimated the US polyurethane foam market at $12.8 billion.
2025-01-01: EPA Technology Transitions rules began restricting polyurethane foam blowing agents to a 150 GWP limit for manufacture and import in covered foam subsectors.
2025: NADA reported 16.2 million US light-duty vehicles sold through franchised dealers, supporting automotive foam demand.
2025: BLS/FRED reported US furniture and related product manufacturing sectoral output of $75.339 billion, down from $85.222 billion in 2022.
2026-06: FRED/BLS reported the plastics material and resin manufacturing PPI at 368.751, up from 308.307 in February 2026.
2026-2034: IMARC forecast the US polyurethane foam market to grow at a 5.15% CAGR to $20.0 billion by 2034.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is cautiously positive but uneven. The strongest growth should come from insulation, packaging, healthcare, EV and automotive lightweighting, and sustainable foam chemistry. Domestic furniture weakness limits flexible foam volumes, while 2026 resin and isocyanate price swings pressure margins. Larger vertically integrated and technology-led manufacturers are better positioned because they can manage raw-material sourcing, meet low-GWP requirements, invest in recycled or bio-based formulations and serve national customers from regional plants. Smaller producers will need niche formulations, fabrication speed or local service advantages to defend margins.
